question: What does the term 'rheumatism' mean in everyday clinical practice?

options.A: An acute injury sustained during heavy physical labor
options.B: A single bacterial infection of the bone marrow
options.C: A complete degeneration of spinal discs from sudden trauma
options.D: Any painful condition affecting joints, muscles, or bones

explanation: Think of rheumatism as a helpful umbrella term! It covers various aches and pains in the musculoskeletal system rather than pointing to just one specific disease. You've got this! [learn more](GNS222_U1_T12#GNS222_U1_T12_h1)

question: How should you think about a patient who comes in with general joint aches and morning stiffness?

options.A: As a routine case of temporary muscle fatigue from hard work
options.B: As a potential entry point into a complex chronic rheumatic condition
options.C: As a clear sign of an acute infectious disease requiring isolation
options.D: As someone suffering from an irreversible nutritional deficiency

explanation: Those early morning stiffness and joint aches are classic clues. They often give us our first hint that a broader inflammatory or joint issue might be developing. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T12#GNS222_U1_T12_h1)

question: What is the name of the smooth inner lining of a joint capsule that gets inflamed in many rheumatic disorders?
explanation: The synovium is the delicate membrane lining our joints. When inflammatory conditions flare up, this lining is usually the main target of the immune response. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T12#GNS222_U1_T12_h2)

question: What damage does pannus formation cause inside an affected joint?

options.A: It repairs damaged muscle fibers rapidly
options.B: It prevents white blood cells from entering the joint
options.C: It releases chemicals that erode cartilage and bone
options.D: It increases natural lubrication to stop friction

explanation: Pannus is an abnormal, thick layer of tissue that creeps across the joint. Sadly, it releases destructive enzymes that chew away at the cartilage and bone. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T12#GNS222_U1_T12_h2)

question: Which rheumatic condition happens when uric acid crystals build up in the joints?
explanation: Gout occurs when excess uric acid forms needle-like crystals in the joints, triggering sudden and very painful flare-ups. Drinking plenty of water and watching diet helps! [learn more](GNS222_U1_T12#GNS222_U1_T12_h3)

question: A patient has widespread body pain, tender points, and ongoing fatigue, but no visible joint swelling. What condition fits best?
explanation: Fibromyalgia is known for widespread pain and tender points, but unlike arthritis, it doesn't cause joint swelling or deformity. Great to keep this distinction in mind! [learn more](GNS222_U1_T12#GNS222_U1_T12_h3)

question: Which lifestyle habit is a known trigger that worsens inflammation in rheumatic conditions?
explanation: Tobacco smoke contains chemicals that fire up the immune system and make inflammation much worse, especially in conditions like rheumatoid arthritis. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T12#GNS222_U1_T12_h4)

question: How does carrying extra body weight lead to osteoarthritis in weight-bearing joints?

options.A: By increasing bone density beyond normal limits
options.B: By blocking blood flow to the synovial lining
options.C: By adding mechanical stress and releasing inflammatory fat proteins
options.D: By causing sudden bacterial infections in the joint capsule

explanation: Extra weight acts like a heavy physical load on knees and hips, while fat tissue also pumps out inflammatory proteins that break down cartilage faster. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T12#GNS222_U1_T12_h4)

question: Which blood test measures general inflammation by checking how fast red blood cells settle?
explanation: Often called ESR, this test watches how quickly red blood cells drop to the bottom of a test tube. Faster settling usually means high inflammation in the body. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T12#GNS222_U1_T12_h5)

question: Why do doctors order antibody blood tests like rheumatoid factor when checking joint pain?

options.A: To evaluate how well the kidneys filter waste products
options.B: To measure the exact daily amount of calcium in the bones
options.C: To determine if the client has an active bacterial wound infection
options.D: To check for specific proteins that indicate an autoimmune attack

explanation: Tests like rheumatoid factor look for rogue proteins that show the immune system is mistakenly attacking the body's own healthy joint tissues. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T12#GNS222_U1_T12_h5)

question: What is the main goal of using disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs)?

options.A: To cure bacterial joint infections within a few days
options.B: To replace lost cartilage with artificial tissue instantly
options.C: To lower blood pressure during acute flare-ups
options.D: To slow down long-term immune-mediated joint damage

explanation: DMARDs help calm down an overactive immune system, protecting the joints from long-term, permanent destruction over time. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T12#GNS222_U1_T12_h6)

question: Why is occupational therapy so helpful for patients with chronic joint disorders?

options.A: It provides surgical joint replacement procedures
options.B: It teaches energy-conservation techniques and assistive devices
options.C: It cures the underlying autoimmune malfunction

explanation: Occupational therapists are wonderful! They teach patients smart ways to protect their joints, save energy, and use handy tools to stay independent. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T12#GNS222_U1_T12_h6)

question: When is the best time to schedule morning care or physical activity for someone with rheumatoid arthritis?

options.A: Early in the morning before any medication is given while stiffness is highest
options.B: Immediately following heavy meals to ensure high energy levels
options.C: Late at night when the client is completely exhausted from the day
options.D: Right after administering morning pain medications and allowing time to take effect

explanation: Giving pain meds a little time to kick in first makes a huge difference! The patient can move around with much less pain and stiffness. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T12#GNS222_U1_T12_h7)

question: A patient complains of a warm, sharp-feeling joint after physical therapy. What is your best nursing action?

options.A: Apply a cold pack to the joint and encourage rest
options.B: Administer a double dose of oral antibiotics immediately
options.C: Apply a warm moist towel to increase blood flow further
options.D: Encourage immediate heavy resistance exercises to push through

explanation: Cold packs are great for calming down a hot, angry joint. They narrow blood vessels, drop acute inflammation, and soothe sharp pain. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T12#GNS222_U1_T12_h7)

question: Which major complication is a well-known risk for patients taking long-term NSAIDs (like ibuprofen)?
explanation: NSAIDs can irritate the stomach lining because they block protective substances called prostaglandins. That's why patients often take them with food or stomach protectors! [learn more](GNS222_U1_T12#GNS222_U1_T12_h8)

question: What is an important joint protection tip you should teach patients to prevent deformities?

options.A: Use larger, stronger joints for lifting and carrying objects
options.B: Wear heavy splints continuously without removing them
options.C: Avoid all movement and stay in bed during flare-ups
options.D: Use smaller finger joints to lift heavy household items

explanation: Smart mechanics! For example, carrying a bag over the forearm instead of gripping it with the fingers protects small hand joints from extra strain and deformity. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T12#GNS222_U1_T12_h8)
